Effectively an unshaded day. Little or no mapped tree cover along the road, and at 3 pm the sun is too high for a ridge to block it. Start early and carry more water than the distance suggests.

The day at a glance

Leaves the irrigated valley floor almost immediately. Most of the day is oak savanna and cattle ranching through Jolon and the Fort Hunter Liggett country — dry-farmed and thinly settled, which is why there is so little on the route. Vineyards reappear on the approach to Paso Robles.

Worth looking up for

  • Remote oak country through Jolon and the Nacimiento backcountry, with no highway miles at all.
  • Lake Nacimiento appears on the descent toward Paso Robles.

What to watch for

  • The hardest day: 62.6 mi and 4,005 ft, with next to no shade on it. Start as early as you can.
  • No water anywhere until Paso Robles at the finish - a 62.6 mi dry stretch, the longest of the trip. Lockwood Store and Diner at mi 25 sits right on the road and is the only thing in the 24.3 mi after mi 0.7. Widening the search to six miles turns up almost nothing else, so unlike day 3 this emptiness is real rather than an artefact of how close a stop has to be to get listed. This is the day the SAG car matters most.
  • The day's biggest climb comes late: mi 42.2–43.8, 639 ft at 7.5%. The steepest is earlier and shorter, mi 10.0–11.5 at 7.7%.

Stops along the way

Mapped in OpenStreetMap and carried in the GPX as waypoints, so they show on a head unit too. Distances are miles from the start. Tap a name for Google Maps, or the arrow for Apple Maps. Not verified on the ground — opening hours and whether a tap actually runs are anyone’s guess. A star marks a stop somebody picked by hand and vouched for, rather than one the OpenStreetMap query happened to return. Everything else here is within a quarter mile of the line; the few that are further say how far.
